_meta: Two perfectly collinear predictors and an outcome, used to show why the individual coefficients of a regression are not identified when the predictors move together -- many different coefficient pairs fit the data exactly equally, so a single coefficient's size or sign carries no meaning -- even though the model's predictions and the SUM of the coefficients are pinned down. When two predictors are collinear (here x2 equals x1 exactly, the extreme of being highly correlated), the fitted value depends only on the combination b1*x1 + b2*x2 = (b1+b2)*x1, so it is a function of the SUM b1+b2 alone. Any pair of coefficients with the same sum produces the identical prediction for every row and therefore the identical residual sum of squares -- the fit cannot tell them apart. This means the sum b1+b2 is identified (the data pins it), but the split between b1 and b2 is not: you can move weight arbitrarily from one to the other, even making one coefficient large and the other negative, without changing the fit at all. So reading an individual coefficient -- 'x2 has a negative effect' -- is meaningless under collinearity, because an equally-good fit gives x2 a positive coefficient; the prediction is trustworthy, the attribution is not. x1 and x2 are the two collinear predictor columns; y is the outcome, generated so the true combined slope is the sum of the coefficients; coeff_pairs is a set of candidate (b1, b2) coefficient pairs to score. These are the fixture; each pair's coefficient sum, its predictions, and its residual sum of squares are computed.
